analysis.one_liner: Sets federal minimum safety standards for sports betting, including addiction safeguards and marketing limits.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors and referred to two House committees, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAFE Bet Act would make sports betting legal nationwide only through state programs that meet federal minimum standards approved by the Department of Justice every three years. States would have to bar bettors under 21 and sports insiders, block credit-card deposits, limit deposits and require income checks for large bettors, ban ads during live games and most of the day, stop operators from using VIP rewards or artificial intelligence to target individual gamblers, and fund treatment for gambling addiction. It would also create a national self-exclusion list and require federal health agencies to track gambling addiction and report on its public health effects.
analysis.who_benefits: People who bet on sports, their families, and communities harmed by problem gambling. The bill would make betting safer by cutting off the tactics operators use to maximize losses: credit-card-funded betting, reload bonuses, VIP rewards tied to how much you gamble, AI-driven individual targeting, and ads beamed at viewers during games. It would give anyone the ability to bar themselves from betting with every operator nationwide with one step, require operators to disclose the true odds of a bet before it is placed, stop operators from blocking or slow-walking withdrawals, and fund treatment and education for gambling disorder.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sports bettors and families hurt by gambling harm

how_it_helps.text: Bettors get affordability checks: no more than 5 deposits per day, no credit-card deposits, and income verification before depositing more than $1,000 a day or $10,000 a month [S3].
Operators must show the actual odds before accepting a bet and let the bettor cancel it at no cost, and must clearly disclose all bonus terms [S3].
Operators cannot hold back winnings as a condition of publicity, cannot cap or delay withdrawals based on how much someone gambled, and cannot charge dormancy fees [S3].
A national self-exclusion list lets a person bar themselves from every approved operator in one step, and operators must fund treatment for gambling disorder [S2] [S3].
Marketing is banned during live game broadcasts and from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m., and 'bonus', 'odds boost', and 'no sweat' offers are barred [S2] [S3].
Federal agencies must survey gambling harm annually, run a national gambling-addiction surveillance system, and have the Surgeon General report on sports betting's public health effects [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sports betting operators (the online sportsbooks), who would lose the highest-margin tools for extracting losses: credit-card betting, reload bonuses, VIP programs, AI micro-targeting, and daytime and in-game advertising. They would also face licensing, background-check, recordkeeping, and reserve requirements, plus a revenue allocation for addiction treatment. Broadcasters and sports media would lose betting-ad revenue during the most valuable windows. Credit card issuers would lose a lending channel to bettors. States that have already legalized betting would have to rewrite their programs to meet federal standards or give them up within 18 months.
analysis.who_pays_short: Online sportsbooks and their advertising channels

drawbacks.text: The bill makes sports wagering federally unlawful outside approved state programs, and the prohibition takes effect 18 months after enactment; states that do not obtain DOJ approval would lose legal betting entirely [S3].

A would-be bettor in a state that does not opt in, or whose program fails federal review, would lose access to legal betting that exists today, and demand could shift to offshore and unlicensed sites, which the bill addresses only through cease-and-desist support [S3].
The framework centralizes decisions in the Attorney General, who approves, renews, and can revoke each state's program, replacing state-level judgments with federal ones every three years [S2] [S3].

Compliance costs — licensing, background checks, recordkeeping, reserve requirements, and treatment funding — would fall on operators and would likely be passed to bettors in worse odds, and heavy restrictions could reduce the sports coverage tax and revenue some states currently collect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and aimed at documented harms: gambling addiction has grown alongside online sports betting since states legalized it after a 2018 Supreme Court decision. The main costs fall on the betting industry and its advertising partners, which is the point. The genuine trade-off is access: the bill treats legal betting as a conditional privilege that states must re-earn, so some bettors would lose legal options if their state does not or cannot meet the standards, and offshore sites are hard to eliminate. The bill does not pair its restrictions with any study of whether legal access itself reduces illicit betting.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Natural Resources committees in March 2025 and has gone no further — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and no other member has signed on.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Tonko (D-NY) introduced the bill on March 11, 2025 [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Committee on Natural Resources [S1] [S5].
No member of the House has cosponsored it [S4].
No further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online sportsbooks and the advertising and credit-card channels around them, which keep today's looser state-by-state rules and the tactics the bill would have banned. Nothing else changed: bettors got no new protections because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online sportsbooks and their ad partners

for.name: Rep. Paul Tonko
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SAFE Bet Act of 2025, establishing federal minimum standards for sports betting and public-health monitoring of gambling harm.

against.name: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee chair with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral; the bill has remained pending in committee.

against.name: Chair, House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup appears in the record.

against.name: Online sports betting operators
against.what_they_did: Have a large financial stake in blocking federal minimum standards; the bill's sponsor's similar prior bill drew industry opposition, and no operator supported this one.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the partisan shape is unknown; the bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no recorded opposition in Congress.

industries.note: The bill strips the industry of its highest-margin growth tools — credit-card deposits, reload bonuses, VIP and tier rewards tied to betting volume, AI-created microbets and individual targeting, and daytime and in-game advertising — and adds licensing, reserve, and treatment-funding costs. The industry's revenue model depends on maximizing individual betting losses, which is exactly what the bill regulates.
Sports betting advertising has become a major revenue source during live game broadcasts, which the bill bans outright, along with all sports-betting ads from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Leagues gain power to restrict bets that threaten contest integrity and, until the end of 2025, operators must use league-licensed data to settle wagers, a valuable licensing right. Leagues also gain protection from insider and proposition betting on amateur and college sports.
The bill bars betting deposits made with credit cards, closing a lending channel into gambling that lets bettors wager money they do not have.

industries.industry: Gambling addiction treatment and research providers
industries.note: Operators must fund treatment and education for gambling disorder, and federal agencies would build a national surveillance system and fund annual research on gambling harm that the industry is barred from conducting or controlling.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no hearing, and a minority-party sponsor, the bill is very unlikely to advance in the 119th Congress; its predecessor version introduced in the previous Congress also died without action. Advancement would require the Energy and Commerce Committee to take it up, which nothing in the record suggests is imminent.
